title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Maritime
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Russia’s APT28 spent at least two months inside a NATO naval shipbuilder’s IT network, Symantec says; no OT impact reported
items.content_text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team reported on 20 October that Swallowtail, the group also tracked as APT28 or Fancy Bear, which the US government links to Russia’s GRU military intelligence, spent at least two months inside the IT network of a naval shipbuilder in a NATO member state. A macro-laden Word attachment opened from Outlook on 24 July installed the Hookedge backdoor. Within a week the operators had a persistent SSH tunnel to their own server, were capturing NTLM credentials and mapping the network, and had loaded a previously undocumented loader whose payload was never recovered. The last activity was seen on 24 September. Symantec found the same group inside a military aircraft-engine maker and a law-enforcement agency, names none of the victims or countries, and does not say data was taken. No OT, ICS or production impact is reported, and Symantec had published no follow-up by 28 October. Editorial assessment: shipyards hold vessel designs and support data, so their business networks are an espionage target in their own right.

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story

items.title: Hackers reportedly reached a US-bound tanker’s propulsion system; no agency has confirmed it, and the FBI reports no disruption
items.content_text: Bloomberg reported on 2 October, citing unnamed US officials, that FBI and Coast Guard investigators found outsiders had briefly accessed digital systems aboard the supertanker VL Prosperity, including its propulsion system, as it approached Texas this summer. Neither agency has confirmed that finding on the record, and how long the access lasted or what the intruders could control is unclear. The FBI says there are no reports of operational disruption, vessel instability, danger to crews or environmental harm. In September the Coast Guard said it had found evidence of a malicious cyber actor aboard. The Liberian-flagged tanker was boarded on 21 August in the Atlantic, per Dragos, after losing communications; its manager, HMM Ocean Service, confirmed the boarding. A second, unnamed tanker was boarded on 24 August. No attacker has been named, and no new official finding had appeared by 28 October.

items.title: FBI and Secret Service say the FortiBleed credential-theft campaign against Fortinet gateways is still active
items.content_text: In a joint advisory dated 6 October, the FBI and US Secret Service warned that attackers are still scanning internet-facing FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways with credentials gathered earlier in the campaign. No vulnerability is involved: the agencies point to reused or leaked passwords and legacy SHA-256 password storage, and researchers describe offline hash cracking and a tool that sniffs login traffic across 24 protocols. Intruders have created rogue admin accounts and deleted or reset legitimate ones, locking owners out, and the access is resold; SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments from it. The agencies say targeted organizations span all 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors, a set that includes transportation systems. SOCRadar’s figure of 86,644 working device credentials across 194 countries dates from 19 June and is not a new count. No maritime or OT victim has been named. Editorial assessment: FortiGate appliances commonly guard links between shipping offices, terminals and remote sites.

items.title: n0n’s deadline for 38 port, shipping and logistics firms passed on 19 October with no leak reported; none has confirmed a breach
items.content_text: The 19 October publication deadline that the data-theft extortion group n0n set for 38 maritime and logistics organizations has passed, and as of 28 October no leak of the data had been reported and no listed organization had confirmed or denied a breach. n0n, first seen in September 2026, posted the batch to its leak site on 12 October, SOCRadar reported; the entries span 18 countries and include 12 port or terminal operators and 10 shipping lines, 12 of them in South Korea. Names reported by The Loadstar and MundoMaritimo include Pusan Newport Co., Busan BNCT, Santos Brasil, Portonave, TTI Algeciras, Eurogate Tanger and Ocean Network Express in Singapore. The group claims EDI messages, manifests, vessel schedules, gate movements and terminal configuration records, and demanded $2.4–14 million in bitcoin. SOCRadar calls every claim unverified and suspects one shared, exposed application rather than 38 separate intrusions; Cydome, quoted by Maritime Executive, pointed to a possible compromise of an environment shared through a maritime software provider, and Cydome’s own interim analysis says at least 21 of the 38 are documented customers of one such vendor, which, per Cydome, has not confirmed an incident. No operational disruption is reported.

items.title: BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day, which Google ties to a suspected China-nexus espionage group, is now in CISA KEV
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS v4.0 9.3), a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 October with a 19 October federal deadline. A day earlier, Google Threat Intelligence Group said the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor it tracks as ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221) had exploited it as a zero-day from late August. SecurityWeek reports two appliances were compromised, one hosted by BeyondTrust and one self-hosted. The intruders gained root, harvested credentials, deleted logs and used the product’s file-transfer feature to pull documents from users’ desktops. BeyondTrust identified the defect on 28 September, shipped a fix on 8 October and had patched its SaaS customers by 9 October; self-hosted customers without automatic updates must patch manually. GTIG names no victims or sectors and advises treating any internet-reachable appliance that ran a vulnerable version during the window as potentially compromised. Editorial assessment: OEMs and service providers use remote-support tools like this to reach vessel and terminal workstations.

items.title: ESET: a Belarus-aligned group’s first documented destructive attack in Europe hit a Ukrainian manufacturer important to transportation; no maritime targets named
items.content_text: ESET’s APT Activity Report for Q2–Q3 2026, published 28 October and covering April to September, says its telemetry shows the Belarus-aligned group FrostyNeighbor attacked a Ukrainian manufacturing company that plays an important role in the country’s transportation sector. ESET calls it the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned actor that it has documented in the European theatre; the report summary gives no malware name, dates or impact details and does not name the company. The report also covers Iran-aligned OilRig subgroups at an Uzbek cellular data provider and North Korea’s DeceptiveDevelopment moving to source-code supply-chain compromise. The published summary does not mention ports, shipping or vessels. Editorial assessment: destructive attacks on transport suppliers are a reminder that shipyards, marine-equipment makers and logistics firms need recovery plans that assume their business systems can be wiped.

items.title: FDD report: Chinese-operated port terminals and patchy cyber oversight expose NATO’s European mobility corridors
items.content_text: A Foundation for Defense of Democracies report by Jiwon Ma, published 28 September, argues that foreign ownership and fragmented cyber oversight weaken the ports, railways and roads NATO would use to move forces across Europe. It says Chinese state-linked firms hold stakes in more than 30 European port terminals and, citing a 2023 European Parliament study, that COSCO Shipping, China Merchants and Hutchison Port Holdings own or operate terminals in roughly half of the EU ports considered critical to NATO. It also finds that civilian transport operators lack consistent security standards across NATO, EU and national authorities, and recommends tighter EU investment screening plus authentication and alternative navigation procedures against satellite interference. The “state-linked” characterization is FDD’s; the report describes structural exposure, not an intrusion at any port.

items.title: PHP2Shell is in CISA KEV, and Palo Alto now reports attacks on internet-exposed PAN-OS firewall management, including PAN-OS on Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 units
items.content_text: CISA added both PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS v4.0 9.2, PHP Group), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 26 October with a 29 October federal deadline. Researchers at Perplexity (Adel Karimi), with Expel’s Marcus Hutchins concurring, confirmed working remote code execution against a honeypot over 24–25 October; no victim organisation has been named, CISA did not describe the activity, and Sophos and Unit 42 withdrew earlier reports of successful exploitation. Palo Alto Networks’ advisory for CVE-2026-109618, raised to Critical on 27 October and updated 28 October, reports active exploitation targeting PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet on PA-Series, VM-Series and Panorama, through the web interface and XML API; GlobalProtect is not affected and no victims are named. Palo Alto scores it CVSS v4.0 9.2, or 5.2 when management access is restricted, and is rolling out hotfixes between 21 and 30 October, some still due on 29–30 October, most of which also cover the Brotli decoder flaw CVE-2026-111497, which CISA added to KEV on 27 October. Siemens SSA-566512 lists RUGGEDCOM APE1808 units running PAN-OS as affected, with remediation through Siemens customer support plus Palo Alto’s workarounds. Schneider Electric’s bulletin SESB-2026-295-01, revised on 26 October, says remediation is now available for EcoStruxure Control Engineering, and Security Expert is fixed in 1.48.4.0; ABB lists B&R’s APROL process control system, with patches planned for 26 and 29 October, and ABB MES installations that use DokuWiki; Rockwell had confirmed no affected products as of its 23 October notice, with its review continuing. PHP itself is fixed in 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. Editorial assessment: Palo Alto firewalls commonly sit between shipping-company, terminal and port business networks and the operational systems behind them, so an exposed management interface is a direct route to the device that enforces that boundary.

items.title: Ivanti Connect Secure: a three-flaw chain gave attackers root on fully patched VPNs, and one link is still unpatched
items.content_text: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that a chain of three flaws gave unauthenticated attackers root on fully patched Connect Secure appliances at a limited number of customers. Two of the flaws are fixed under one CVE, CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS v3.1 8.6), which CISA added to KEV the same day with a 16 October deadline; the third, a privilege-escalation bug, still had no Ivanti fix as of 28 October. Volexity found the chain during an incident response and tracks a new actor, UTA0576; exploitation dates from at least early October, with Volexity and Defused placing it at 1–3 October. The intruders left no web shell, stole domain credentials, queried Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, sprayed passwords and wiped logs. Volexity and CISA warn that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker may not detect the compromise. Editorial assessment: Connect Secure is a common remote-access gateway for shipping offices, terminal operators and their vendors.

items.title: Citrix NetScaler: a fourth critical flaw follows three exploited zero-days, and recently patched SAML appliances need another upgrade
items.content_text: Citrix disclosed a fourth critical NetScaler ADC and Gateway flaw on 8 October in bulletin CTX697191: CVE-2026-107406 (CVSS v4.0 9.5), a memory overflow on appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider that Citrix says may lead to remote code execution or denial of service. No exploitation of it has been reported and it is not in KEV, but builds that fixed the September zero-days (14.1-73.37 to 73.41 and 13.1-64.23 to 64.28) stay vulnerable when used as a SAML IdP, so those appliances need another upgrade. Three earlier flaws are exploited and in KEV: CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 (both CVSS 9.5, added 27 September) and CVE-2026-88779 (added 4 October), which Citrix and watchTowr describe as a denial-of-service bug. Cybersecurity Dive reported on 12 October that CISA again urged patching, warning that attackers use 88779 to force reboots so code planted through 88771 runs. Mandiant links the activity only to suspected state-nexus actors and counts dozens of affected organizations; Arctic Wolf tracks at least 78 targeted organizations, and Shadowserver sees more than 20,000 exposed or potentially vulnerable appliances. Editorial assessment: NetScaler Gateway is a common remote-access front door into port, terminal and OT DMZ networks.

items.title: Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator: an exploited flaw that gives any logged-in user operator rights is in CISA KEV, and the federal deadline has passed
items.content_text: Arista disclosed on 22 October, in Security Advisory 0199, that CVE-2026-114625, an SQL injection flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator, is being actively exploited: any authenticated user can use it to gain operator privileges on the orchestrator. Arista, as CVE numbering authority, scores it CVSS v3.1 9.9 and v4.0 9.4. CISA added it to KEV on 23 October with a 26 October federal deadline, which has now passed. Fixed releases are 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12, and Arista-hosted orchestrators are already patched. SecurityWeek reports it is the third exploited orchestrator zero-day in four months. No victim, sector or actor has been named. Editorial assessment: where terminals, remote port facilities or ship-management offices connect over a VeloCloud SD-WAN, the orchestrator holds every site’s edge configuration, so whoever controls it could open paths into the networks behind those sites.

items.title: FortiOS flaw from Unit 42’s Peerstitch case is in CISA KEV; a telecom MSP’s compromise exposed configurations of more than 500 managed FortiGates
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2025-61624, a FortiOS command-line path-traversal flaw, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 October with a 19 October federal deadline. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 reported on 14 October that intruders it tracks as CL-STA-0954 (also UNC5820) got into a telecommunications managed service provider through FortiManager flaw CVE-2024-47575, then used CVE-2025-61624 to gain root on managed FortiGate firewalls and plant a loader it calls PEERSTITCH. Configuration and credential material for more than 500 managed FortiGates was exposed; Unit 42 says that is exposure, not confirmed intrusion into those customers’ networks, and it names no state behind the cluster. Fortinet fixed the flaw in April 2026 and rates it Medium because it requires privileged, authenticated access; FortiProxy, FortiPAM and FortiSwitchManager are also affected. The CVE record lists Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808, a rugged application platform that can run FortiOS, as affected too. Editorial assessment: shipping companies and terminal operators whose FortiGates are run by an MSP share that provider’s FortiManager exposure.

items.title: Siemens Software Center: a DLL side-loading flaw is exploited in a ClickFix campaign and added to CISA KEV; update to V4.0.9.8
items.content_text: Siemens confirmed on 19 October that CVE-2026-110936, an uncontrolled-search-path flaw in Siemens Software Center (CVSS v3.1 6.7, v4.0 8.4), is being exploited in what it calls the “Romulus” multi-platform ClickFix campaign. Attackers bundle a genuine, validly signed Software Center executable with their own DLLs and trick users into running it, so the trusted program loads the attackers’ code. Siemens says no Siemens system, product or update channel was breached, and it names no final malware family. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 20 October with a 3 November deadline and on 22 October republished Siemens’ advisory as ICSA-26-295-03, listing Transportation Systems among the affected sectors. All versions before V4.0.9.8 are affected; that release fixes the flaw, and existing installations update automatically on next start. Exploitation needs a user to run the attackers’ bundle locally; it does not reach automation equipment over the network. Editorial assessment: the exposure sits on the engineering laptops that maintain Siemens automation at terminals and aboard vessels.

items.title: SonicWall SMA1000: honeypots logged attempts against a CVSS 10 pre-authentication flaw two days after the fix
items.content_text: SonicWall fixed CVE-2026-102255 on 6 October (advisory SNWLID-2026-0017): a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the SMA1000 WorkPlace interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker make the appliance send requests to its own internal functions. CISA’s enrichment scores it CVSS v3.1 10.0, and SonicWall calls it maximum severity. Defused saw the first hits on its decoys on 8 October and Previdian counted 135 attempts from two US addresses, SecurityWeek reported on 12 October; neither has shown that any attempt succeeded. Some threat feeds now label the flaw exploited, but no successful exploitation had been confirmed as of 28 October, and it is not in KEV as of CISA’s 27 October catalog. Affected are SMA 6210, 7210 and 8200v appliances on 12.4.3-03526 or 12.5.0-02952 and earlier; SMA 100 and firewall SSL-VPN are not affected. Three authenticated flaws were fixed alongside it, and SMA1000 has been repeatedly exploited in 2026. Editorial assessment: these appliances often give integrators and OEMs a path toward port and fleet-support networks.

items.title: Toptech TMS7 and TopHAT: ten flaws up to CVSS 10.0 in terminal-management software, fixed in release 7.8
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-272-02 (29 September) covers ten vulnerabilities in Toptech Systems TMS7 and TopHAT 7.6.3. The most severe, CVE-2026-71379 (CVSS 10.0), leaves files and directories accessible to external parties; CVE-2026-70356 (9.1) allows unrestricted file upload, and five SQL-injection flaws score 9.0. CISA says exploitation could let an attacker access critical data or execute arbitrary code, and lists the Energy, Chemical and Transportation Systems sectors, with deployments worldwide. Toptech notified customers on 20 July and fixed all the issues in release 7.8. CISA reports no known public exploitation. Editorial assessment: Toptech’s terminal-management software is used at fuel and bulk-liquid terminals, including those in ports, so marine terminal operators should check whether they run it.

items.title: Moxa: its Remote Connect client could be fooled by a fake server, and the end-of-life OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway will get no fix
items.content_text: Moxa published advisory MPSA-269510 on 27 October covering two products used to reach remote field equipment. CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6, scored by Moxa) is an improper certificate-validation flaw in the Moxa Remote Connect Suite client (MRC Client) 1.0.0 through 4.2.0: an attacker positioned between the client and its server could impersonate the server, which supplies the client’s OpenVPN configuration, and read or alter the traffic. Version 4.2.2 fixes it and is obtained through Moxa technical support. The OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway has static HTTPS and CA private keys in its firmware (CVE-2026-111460, v4.0 7.7) and an OS command injection reachable through SMS management by an attacker with high privileges (CVE-2026-111461, v4.0 7.5). Moxa considers the gateway end-of-life and will not fix it; the mitigations are resetting the device to regenerate its keys and keeping SMS management disabled, which is the default. No exploitation has been reported. Editorial assessment: remote-connect clients and cellular gateways like these link remote port-side equipment and terminal sites back to engineers and vendors, so unsupported units should be retired rather than left in place.

items.title: Moxa AIG-302 edge gateways: a hard-coded cryptographic key and a missing-authorization flaw are fixed in firmware 1.4.1
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-293-03 (20 October) covers two flaws in Moxa AIG-302 IIoT gateways running ThingsPro Edge firmware 1.4.0 and earlier: CVE-2026-109813, a hard-coded cryptographic key (CVSS v3.1 8.1, v4.0 8.6), and CVE-2026-109812, missing authorization (v3.1 6.8, v4.0 6.9). Moxa fixed both in firmware 1.4.1 (advisory MPSA-262560). CISA lists Critical Manufacturing, Energy and Water and Wastewater as affected sectors and reports no known exploitation. Separately, Moxa’s notice MPSA-260001 (22 October) concerns the PHP2Shell flaws in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), which are now in CISA KEV (see the PHP2Shell card above); its contents could not be verified for this edition, so check it directly for the status of Moxa products. Editorial assessment: Moxa gateways and device servers are common in terminal and shipboard networks, so fleets and terminals running AIG-302 units should schedule the update.

items.title: Lantronix G520 cellular gateways: a leaked signing key lets attackers push trusted firmware; update to 2.6.0.7R6
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-272-01 (29 September) covers two flaws in Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateways running 2.6.0.4R6_stable, each CVSS 7.5 (v3.1). CVE-2026-91191 is a signature-verification failure in the update mechanism: per the advisory, the publicly distributed SDK contains the production private key, so an attacker could sign malicious packages the gateway will trust. CVE-2026-84409 is a cross-site scripting flaw in how the web interface displays update metadata fetched over plain HTTP. CISA says exploitation could let an attacker replace software and run code with root privileges, and lists Transportation Systems, Energy and Water and Wastewater among affected sectors. Lantronix fixed both in firmware 2.6.0.7R6; no exploitation has been reported. Editorial assessment: cellular gateways like these often link remote port-side equipment and terminal sensors back to control centers.

items.title: MARAD renews its warning on Chinese port technology as Advisory 2026-014, with crane-network hardening steps
items.content_text: The US Maritime Administration issued MSCI Advisory 2026-014, “Worldwide: Foreign Adversarial Technological, Physical, and Cyber Influence,” on 21 October; it cancels and replaces Advisory 2026-007 and runs to 19 April 2027. It repeats three warnings. China’s state-supported LOGINK logistics platform likely gives China access to sensitive logistics data, and US law bars federal entities and federally funded US companies from using it. Nuctech, a Chinese state-controlled maker of inspection scanners on the Commerce Entity List, sells equipment that can access biometric, personal, cargo and geolocation data. ZPMC, which holds the largest global share of the ship-to-shore crane market, makes cranes that, depending on configuration, may be remotely controlled, serviced or programmed. MARAD alleges no specific compromise. Its guidance includes complying with Coast Guard MARSEC Directives 105-4 and 105-5, segmenting crane networks from business networks, requiring multi-factor authentication for remote access, monitoring all crane traffic, running periodic PLC program integrity checks, and keeping offline backups and spare hardware.

items.title: Class societies, maritime security vendors and MTS-ISAC launch the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository for ship and port IT/OT flaws
items.content_text: A coalition calling itself the Blue Initiative, made up of Cydome, Rakuten Maritime, the classification societies Bureau Veritas and ClassNK, and the Maritime Transportation System ISAC (MTS-ISAC), launched the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository on or before 26 October, Infosecurity Magazine reported that day. It is billed as the first database to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the maritime sector. Researchers from Cydome and the other partners validate proposed entries before publication, and Infosecurity says vulnerabilities are published only once a patch is available. Users can browse CVEs, filter by equipment or vendor, read expert analysis and subscribe to alerts. Cydome’s chief executive describes the aim as a “public and open single source of truth” for maritime vulnerabilities. SecurityWeek, which describes the database as free, also reports entry counts that could not be verified independently, so they are left out here. It is a resource, not a new threat. Editorial assessment: it gives ship managers and terminal operators a maritime-specific list to check assets against, but because it waits for a patch, vendor PSIRTs and CISA ICS advisories remain the place to learn about unfixed flaws.

items.title: Coast Guard issues NVIC 02-26 on meeting its maritime cyber rule; plans, assessments and Cybersecurity Officer designations are due 16 July 2027
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard’s Navigation and Vessel Inspection Circular 02-26, dated 19 October and reported by Industrial Cyber on 23 October, explains how to comply with the cybersecurity requirements in 33 CFR Part 101 Subpart F for US-flagged vessels, MTSA-regulated facilities and Outer Continental Shelf facilities. It covers designating a Cybersecurity Officer, carrying out the cybersecurity assessment, which includes identifying critical IT and OT systems and how they depend on each other, and writing and submitting a Cybersecurity Plan; all three are due to the Coast Guard by 16 July 2027. Enclosures include a sample designation letter, an optional NIST CSF-based method for filtering risk, and penetration-testing guidance, including OT safety, for the five-year renewal cycle; testing is not required for the first plan. The approach is performance-based: the Coast Guard will not prescribe products, and operators need not hire third parties. An NVIC is guidance and does not change the rule’s deadlines.
